tribal_nations.name: Burns Paiute Tribe
aliases: Wada Tika Band of Northern Paiute
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Burns Paiute Indian Colony and Reservation, Harney County, southeastern Oregon
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Separate sovereign. Wadatika Band of the Northern Paiute (Numa) people. One of several Northern Paiute bands whose traditional territory spans the High Desert and Great Basin of southeastern Oregon. Forced onto reservation after the Bannock War (1878). Reservation established 1972. The Wadatika resisted removal and maintained presence in their homeland through extraordinary persistence. Language: Northern Paiute (Numa), Uto-Aztecan family, critically endangered. Tribal programs include language revitalization, natural resources, health, and housing.
tribal_nations.treaty_basis: Treaty of 1868 (Northern Paiute); Indian Reorganization Act 1934; Restoration through federal acknowledgment
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: High Desert and Great Basin of southeastern Oregon; Harney Basin; Malheur Lake; Steens Mountain region

tribal_nations.name: Confederated Tribes of Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw Indians
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Coos Bay area and southwestern Oregon coast; Coos, Douglas, Lane Counties
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Separate sovereign. Confederacy of three distinct peoples with separate languages: Hanis Coos and Miluk Coos (two dialects of the Coosan language family — language isolate), Lower Umpqua (Quuiich — Siuslawan language family), and Siuslaw (Shayuustees — Siuslawan family). The Coos Bay Treaty of 1855 was signed but never ratified by Congress — a deliberate act of erasure. People were removed to the Coast Reservation. Terminated by federal government 1954 — one of the most unjust terminations in Oregon history. Federal recognition restored 1984 through the Cow Creek-CTCLUSI Restoration Act. Languages are among the rarest in North America — all four are language isolates with no known relatives. Active revitalization at ctclusi.org language programs.
tribal_nations.treaty_basis: Coos Bay Treaty 1855 (signed but never ratified by U.S. Senate — treaty rights violated)
tribal_nations.language_family: Coosan (language isolate family); Siuslawan (language isolate family)
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Oregon coast from Florence south through Coos Bay; lower Umpqua River valley; lower Siuslaw River valley

tribal_nations.name: Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Grand Ronde Reservation, Polk and Yamhill Counties; service area statewide Oregon
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Separate sovereign. One of the most complex confederacies in North America — over 27 distinct tribal groups and bands forcibly relocated to Grand Ronde beginning 1856. Constituent peoples include: Tualatin/Atfalati Kalapuya, Yamhill Kalapuya, Santiam Kalapuya (Upper and Lower), Mary's River Kalapuya, Long Tom Kalapuya, Yoncalla Kalapuya, Calapooia Kalapuya, Muddy Creek Kalapuya, Chelamela, Chemapho; Molalla (Molale); Umpqua; Nehalem Tillamook, Tillamook proper, Nestucca, Salmon River, Siletz Tillamook; Clatsop Chinook; Shoalwater Bay Chinook; Rogue River peoples; Upper Umpqua; Galice-Applegate Athabaskan; and others. The Willamette Valley — Kalapuya homeland — was stripped of its people in a matter of years. The Kalapuya practiced controlled burning for camas and tarweed management — their stewardship created the fertile valley settlers coveted. Terminated 1954 — catastrophic. Restored 1983. Chinuk Wawa (the Oregon trade language) became the living community language and is now actively taught. The tribe runs one of the most respected language programs in Indian Country.
tribal_nations.treaty_basis: Dayton Treaty 1855 (Kalapuya); multiple other treaties — many unratified or violated
tribal_nations.language_family: Multiple — Kalapuyan; Salishan (Tillamook); Athabaskan; Chinookan; Shastan; Takelman; Penutian
tribal_nations.language_name: Chinuk Wawa (living community language); Tualatin-Yamhill Kalapuya; Molalla; Tillamook; multiple others
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Willamette Valley (primary Kalapuya homeland); Coast Range; northern Oregon coast (Tillamook); Columbia River (Clatsop)
tribal_nations.address: 9615 Grand Ronde Rd, Grand Ronde OR 97347

tribal_nations.name: Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Siletz Reservation, Lincoln County; service area extends statewide Oregon
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Separate sovereign. Confederacy of over 27 southwestern Oregon tribal groups forcibly concentrated on the Coast Reservation beginning 1855 — one of the largest and most culturally diverse forced relocations in Pacific Northwest history. Constituent peoples include: Nehalem Tillamook, Tillamook proper, Nestucca, Salmon River, Siletz Tillamook (Salishan); Yaquina (Yakonan); Alsea/Alsean (Yakonan); Siuslaw; Lower Umpqua; Coos; Tututni (Athabaskan); Chetco (Athabaskan); Coquille upper bands; Galice-Applegate (Athabaskan); Dakubetede Athabaskan; Shasta Costa; Takelma; Latgawa; Upper Umpqua; and others. Original Coast Reservation was 1.1 million acres — reduced to ~3,600 acres through a series of executive orders over decades. Terminated 1954 in another catastrophic act of erasure. Restored 1977. Multiple language revitalization programs — Tillamook, Takelma, Athabaskan dialects, Alsean.
tribal_nations.treaty_basis: Dayton Treaty 1855; Coast Treaty 1855; multiple treaties — most unratified or violated by U.S.
tribal_nations.language_family: Multiple — Salishan; Athabaskan (Oregon Coast branch); Coosan; Siuslawan; Shastan; Takelman; Yakonan
tribal_nations.language_name: Tillamook (Salishan); Tututni; Chetco; Takelma; Alsea; multiple others
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Oregon coast from Columbia River to California border; Coast Range; Rogue, Chetco, Illinois, Applegate, Umpqua watersheds

tribal_nations.name: Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Umatilla Indian Reservation, Umatilla County, northeastern Oregon; ceded territory across OR, WA, ID
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Separate sovereign. Three distinct peoples confederated: Cayuse (Liksiyu — 'Superior People'), Umatilla (Imatalamłáma — 'People of the Many Rocks'), and Walla Walla (Waluulapam — 'People of the River'). The Walla Walla Council of 1855 was one of the most consequential treaty negotiations in Pacific Northwest history — 5,000 Native people attended. Treaty reserved explicit rights to fish, hunt, gather, and pasture livestock at all usual and accustomed places across the ceded territory spanning present-day OR, WA, and ID — rights that remain legally enforceable today. The Cayuse were master horsemen and played a central role in the Columbia Plateau trade network. Celilo Falls fishing rights are part of the reserved treaty rights. CTUIR operates one of the most advanced tribal natural resource management programs in North America, including groundbreaking environmental restoration work. Languages: Cayuse (language isolate — moribund, deep revitalization efforts), Umatilla Sahaptin and Walla Walla Sahaptin (Ichishkíin Sínwit — Sahaptian family, plateau Penutian). Active Ichishkíin language program.
tribal_nations.treaty_basis: Treaty with the Walla Walla, Cayuse, etc. 1855 (Walla Walla Council) — 12 Stat. 945
tribal_nations.language_family: Cayuse: language isolate; Sahaptian (Plateau Penutian branch)
tribal_nations.language_name: Cayuse; Umatilla Sahaptin (Ichishkíin); Walla Walla Sahaptin (Ichishkíin)
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Columbia Plateau: Blue Mountains, Umatilla River, Columbia River from Wallula Gap west, Walla Walla River drainage, Snake River confluence region

tribal_nations.name: Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs Reservation of Oregon
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Warm Springs Reservation, Jefferson and Wasco Counties, north-central Oregon; ceded territory across north-central OR and southern WA
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Separate sovereign. Three distinct peoples: Warm Springs (Sahaptin-speaking confederated bands — Tenino/Warm Springs, Tyigh, Wyam, Dock-Spus); Wasco (Kiksht-speaking Chinookan people — major traders at The Dalles trade center, the crossroads of the Pacific Northwest trade network); and Northern Paiute (Numa — added to reservation 1879 after being displaced from their own homeland in the Bannock War). Treaty of 1855 at Wasco. Reservation is 1,059 square miles — one of the largest in Oregon. Celilo Falls — Wyam fishing village and one of the most important salmon fishing and trading sites in North America for at least 11,000 years — was permanently drowned by The Dalles Dam on March 10, 1957, in less than 24 hours. The Army Corps of Engineers paid $26.8 million. No amount could compensate for the loss. The Wyam wept on the bank as their world was destroyed. Their reserved fishing rights remain legally in force downstream. Languages: Warm Springs Sahaptin (Ichishkíin — Sahaptian family), Kiksht (Wasco-Wishram Chinookan — Chinookan family), Northern Paiute (Numa — Uto-Aztecan). All endangered. Revitalization active.
tribal_nations.treaty_basis: Treaty with the Tribes of Middle Oregon 1855 — 12 Stat. 963
tribal_nations.language_name: Warm Springs Sahaptin (Ichishkíin); Kiksht (Wasco Chinookan); Northern Paiute (Numa)
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Columbia Plateau from eastern Cascades: Deschutes River; Columbia River from Celilo to Cascades; Warm Springs River; White River; Tygh Valley; The Dalles trade center (Wasco)
tribal_nations.historical_note: Celilo Falls (Wy-am) — drowned March 10, 1957 by The Dalles Dam over tribal objection. One of the most devastating acts of cultural and ecological destruction in Oregon history.
tribal_nations.address: P.O. Box C, Warm Springs OR 97761

tribal_nations.name: Coquille Indian Tribe
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Coquille tribal lands, Coos County; North Bend/Coos Bay area, southwestern Oregon coast
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Separate sovereign. The Coquille (Mishikhwutmetunne — 'people of the south wind') are an Athabaskan-speaking people of the Coquille River and southern Oregon coast. Their territory extended from the lower Coquille River to the coast and into the Coast Range. Suffered devastating population collapse through disease, violence, and removal. Terminated 1954 — unjust. Restored 1989 through the Coquille Indian Tribe Restoration Act. Known for innovative social justice policies — the Coquille were one of the first tribes in the U.S. to extend tribal marriage rights to same-sex couples (2008). Language: Upper Coquille (Athabaskan — Oregon Coast Athabaskan branch) and Lower Coquille (Miluk Coos). Both critically endangered.
tribal_nations.treaty_basis: Unratified treaty rights; Coast Treaty 1855 (part of larger Coast Reservation process)
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Coquille River drainage; southern Oregon coast from Cape Arago to Floras Creek
tribal_nations.historical_note: First tribal nation in the U.S. to extend marriage equality to same-sex couples under tribal law (2008).

tribal_nations.name: Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Roseburg area, Douglas County, southwestern Oregon; service area extends across southwestern Oregon
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Separate sovereign. The Cow Creek Band are an Upper Umpqua Athabaskan people — Nahankhuotana, 'people of the upper Umpqua.' Their territory centered on the upper South Umpqua River and its tributaries in the rugged interior of southwestern Oregon. Treaty of September 19, 1853 — one of the earliest Oregon treaties. The treaty was ratified but the government failed to implement it for decades. Terminated 1954 — devastatingly unjust for a people with a ratified treaty. Restored 1982 — the first Oregon tribe restored through individual legislation, paving the way for others. The tribe has become known for aggressive economic development reinvested in community services. Language: Upper Umpqua (Oregon Coast Athabaskan — also called Nahankuhotana Athabaskan). Critically endangered. Revitalization active.
tribal_nations.restoration_act: Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Indian Tribe Restoration Act 1982
tribal_nations.treaty_basis: Treaty with the Umpqua — Cow Creek Band, September 19, 1853 — 10 Stat. 1027
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Upper South Umpqua River valley and tributaries; interior Coast Range of southwestern Oregon
tribal_nations.historical_note: First Oregon tribe restored through individual federal legislation (1982), establishing the legal precedent for subsequent Oregon restorations.
tribal_nations.address: 2371 NE Stephens St Suite 100, Roseburg OR 97470

tribal_nations.name: Klamath Tribes
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Klamath County, south-central Oregon; traditional territory spans OR-CA border region
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Separate sovereign. Three distinct peoples: Klamath (Maklaks — 'people of the lake'), Modoc (Moatokni Maklaks — 'people of the south'), and Yahooskin Band of Snake Paiute (Northern Paiute). The Klamath Basin is one of the most ecologically rich regions in the Pacific Northwest — home to Klamath Lake, C'waam (Lost River sucker) and Koptu (shortnose sucker) fish that are sacred and central to Klamath identity. Treaty of 1864 reserved 2.2 million acres. The Klamath Tribes suffered one of the most devastating terminations in American Indian history — Termination Act of 1954 stripped 2.2 million acres of old-growth forest. The land was sold or transferred. Restored 1986 — but without the land base, which was never fully returned. The tribe continues to fight for Klamath River dam removal (achieved 2023-2024 — the largest dam removal in U.S. history, an extraordinary victory) and restoration of reserved water and fish rights. The C'waam and Koptu remain endangered. Languages: Klamath-Modoc (Klamath — language isolate or Plateau Penutian, contested); Yahooskin Northern Paiute (Uto-Aztecan). Both endangered. The Klamath-Modoc language has a small number of speakers and an active revitalization program.
tribal_nations.treaty_basis: Treaty with the Klamath, etc. October 14, 1864 — 16 Stat. 707
tribal_nations.language_family: Klamath-Modoc: language isolate (possibly Plateau Penutian); Yahooskin: Uto-Aztecan
tribal_nations.language_name: Klamath (Maklaks language); Modoc; Yahooskin Northern Paiute
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Klamath Basin including Klamath Lake, Upper Klamath Lake, Agency Lake, Williamson River, Sprague River, Lost River; extending into northern California (Modoc territory)
tribal_nations.historical_note: Klamath River dam removal (2023-2024) — largest dam removal in U.S. history — was led in significant part by the Klamath Tribes. A historic victory for tribal sovereignty and salmon recovery after decades of advocacy.

tribal_nations.name: Chinook Indian Nation
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Columbia River mouth region, southwestern Washington and northwestern Oregon; Willapa Bay area
tribal_nations.notes: Pending federal recognition — recognition has been unjustly denied for decades despite clear historical, genealogical, and cultural continuity. The Chinook are the people of the lower Columbia River — one of the most geographically and economically significant river systems in North America. Their trade language (Chinuk Wawa) became the dominant inter-tribal and fur-trade language of the Pacific Northwest. The Chinook met Lewis and Clark at the river's mouth in 1805. The federal government vacillated on recognition — a proposed rule granting recognition was finalized in the final days of the Clinton administration, then rescinded by the Bush administration in 2002. An extraordinary injustice. The Chinook people never stopped existing. Language: Chinookan (Lower Chinook / Chinook proper — Chinookan language family). Chinuk Wawa revitalization active through Grand Ronde's program. The Chinook language itself is being revitalized.
tribal_nations.recognition_notes: Federal recognition rescinded 2002 after Clinton administration grant. Ongoing advocacy. State of Washington recognizes the Chinook.
tribal_nations.treaty_basis: No ratified treaty — treaty rights claimed through sustained historical presence and 1851 Anson Dart unratified treaties
tribal_nations.language_name: Chinook (Lower Chinook); Chinuk Wawa (trade language, now community language at Grand Ronde)
tribal_nations.language_status: critically_endangered; Chinuk Wawa revitalized at Grand Ronde
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Lower Columbia River from Cascade Range to the Pacific; Columbia River mouth; Willapa Bay; Shoalwater Bay

tribal_nations.name: Kalapuya People (Non-enrolled / Landless communities)
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Willamette Valley, Oregon — from Portland south through Eugene and beyond
tribal_nations.notes: Community nation — Kalapuya descendants who are enrolled in the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde or Siletz, or who remain in Willamette Valley communities not enrolled. The Kalapuya (or Kalapooian peoples) are the original inhabitants of the Willamette Valley — one of the most fertile and contested landscapes in Oregon history. Multiple distinct Kalapuya bands/peoples: Tualatin (Atfalati), Yamhill, Santiam (Upper and Lower), Mary's River (Ampinefu), Long Tom, Yoncalla, Calapooia, Muddy Creek, Chelamela, Chemapho, and others. The Kalapuya practiced sophisticated landscape management through controlled burning — their stewardship created the open prairies and camas fields that made the Willamette Valley what settlers found. Disease destroyed up to 90% of the Kalapuya population before formal removal. All surviving Kalapuya were removed to Grand Ronde and Siletz. Languages: Tualatin-Yamhill; Santiam; Yoncalla; and other Kalapuyan dialects — Kalapuyan language family. All critically endangered.
tribal_nations.treaty_basis: Dayton Treaty 1855; multiple Kalapuya treaties — all removed to Grand Ronde
tribal_nations.language_name: Tualatin-Yamhill; Santiam Kalapuya; Yoncalla; multiple dialects
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Willamette Valley entire extent — Portland Basin south through Eugene, Roseburg area (Yoncalla); including Coast Range western slopes
tribal_nations.enrollment_contact: See Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde

tribal_nations.name: Coeur d'Alene Tribe
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Coeur d'Alene Reservation, Benewah and Kootenai Counties, northern Idaho; Lake Coeur d'Alene region
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Separate sovereign. The Coeur d'Alene call themselves Schitsu'umsh — 'the discovered people' or 'those who are found here.' Their territory centered on Lake Coeur d'Alene (Hnchin'rih'um — 'the heart of the lake people's land'), one of the most beautiful mountain lakes in North America. The name 'Coeur d'Alene' (meaning 'heart of an awl' or 'sharp-hearted') was given by French fur traders, presumably referring to the tribe's reputation as sharp traders. The Schitsu'umsh were expert fishermen and camas gatherers. The Executive Order of 1873 established the reservation. The tribe lost most of Lake Coeur d'Alene and surrounding land; decades of legal battles resulted in a 2001 Idaho Supreme Court ruling that awarded the tribe the bed and banks of the southern third of the lake — a landmark victory. The Bunker Hill Superfund Site contaminated tribal waters for decades. Language: Coeur d'Alene (Schitsu'umsh language — Interior Salish, Salishan family). Critically endangered — estimated fewer than 20 fluent speakers in recent years. One of the most active and innovative language revitalization programs in Idaho, including immersion schools.
tribal_nations.treaty_basis: Executive Order 1873; Treaty of 1858 (unratified); recognized through Indian Reorganization Act 1934
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Lake Coeur d'Alene and surrounding region; Spokane River; St. Joe River; Palouse River headwaters; into present-day Washington and Montana
tribal_nations.historical_note: 2001 Idaho Supreme Court decision granted the tribe ownership of the bed and banks of the southern third of Lake Coeur d'Alene — one of the most significant tribal water rights victories in Idaho history.

tribal_nations.name: Kootenai Tribe of Idaho
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Kootenai Reservation, Boundary County, northern Idaho; Bonners Ferry area
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Separate sovereign. The Kootenai (Ktunaxa in their own language — pronounced 'k-too-NAH-ha') are a distinct people whose language is a language isolate — unrelated to any other known language family on earth. Their territory spans what is now northern Idaho, northwestern Montana, northeastern Washington, and southern British Columbia (where Ktunaxa First Nations remain). The Idaho Kootenai are one of the smallest federally recognized tribes in the United States — fewer than 200 members. In 1974, facing extreme poverty and the U.S. government's failure to honor its obligations, the Kootenai Tribe of Idaho declared war on the United States — and set up roadblocks charging tolls. This act of extraordinary courage, at a moment of desperation, brought national attention and resulted in a small land purchase by Congress. The tribe used that land as the nucleus for economic development. Language: Ktunaxa (Kutenai — language isolate, no known relatives). Severely endangered. Cross-border revitalization with Canadian Ktunaxa First Nations.
tribal_nations.treaty_basis: No formal treaty; recognized through federal acknowledgment
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Kootenay River drainage; Kootenay Lake (BC); Pend Oreille River; Columbia River headwaters; northern Idaho panhandle
tribal_nations.historical_note: 1974: Kootenai Tribe declared war on the United States and set up roadblocks to protest poverty and government neglect. The action brought national attention and resulted in Congressional appropriations for a small land purchase.

tribal_nations.name: Nez Perce Tribe
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Nez Perce Reservation, Clearwater, Idaho, Lewis, and Nez Perce Counties, central Idaho; ceded territory across ID, OR, WA
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Separate sovereign. The Nez Perce call themselves Niimíipuu — 'the real people' or 'we the people.' Their territory in the Plateau bioregion was one of the largest of any Pacific Northwest tribe, spanning the Clearwater and Salmon River country of Idaho, the Grande Ronde Valley of Oregon, and the Snake River region. The Niimíipuu were master horsemen — the Appaloosa horse breed is named for the Palouse River country of the Nez Perce. The Walla Walla Treaty of 1855 established the original reservation; the Lapwai Treaty of 1863 unilaterally reduced the reservation by 90% without consent of many chiefs — this 'thief treaty' caused the split between 'treaty' and 'non-treaty' Nez Perce. Chief Joseph (Hinmaton-Yalaktit, 'Thunder Rolling in the Mountains') and his band's 1,700-mile flight from the Army in 1877 — through Oregon, Idaho, Wyoming, and Montana, nearly reaching the Canadian border — is one of the most extraordinary military campaigns and human stories in North American history. Chief Joseph's surrender speech is among the most powerful statements of Indigenous sovereignty ever recorded. Reserved treaty rights include fishing at all usual and accustomed places — rights actively enforced today. Language: Nez Perce (Niimíiput — Sahaptian family, Plateau Penutian branch). Endangered. Active revitalization including immersion programs.
tribal_nations.treaty_basis: Treaty of 1855 (Walla Walla Council); Lapwai Treaty 1863 (contested — 'thief treaty' — signed by minority of chiefs)
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Clearwater River; Salmon River; Snake River; Grande Ronde Valley (OR); Wallowa Valley (OR); Palouse Country (WA); Bitterroot Mountains
tribal_nations.historical_note: Chief Joseph's flight of 1877 — 1,700 miles across four present-day states with 800 people (700 non-combatants) pursued by the U.S. Army — ended 40 miles from the Canadian border. Chief Joseph's words at surrender: 'Hear me, my chiefs! I am tired. My heart is sick and sad. From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever.'

tribal_nations.name: Shoshone-Bannock Tribes of the Fort Hall Reservation
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Fort Hall Reservation, Bingham and Power Counties, southeastern Idaho; Snake River Plain region
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Separate sovereign. Two distinct peoples confederated: Shoshone (Newe — 'the people,' specifically the Northern and Eastern Shoshone bands) and Bannock (Banak — Northern Paiute people who adopted the horse and migrated onto the Snake River Plain). Together they controlled a vast territory across southern Idaho, northern Nevada, and adjacent areas. The Fort Bridger Treaty of 1868 established reservation rights. Fort Hall Reservation established 1868 — originally much larger, reduced over time. The Shoshone-Bannock are buffalo hunters, fishermen (Snake River salmon), and root gatherers. The Fort Hall Indian Reservation is home to one of the premier rodeos in the West — Fort Hall Indian Days. The Shoshone-Bannock retain reserved fishing rights in the Snake River and its tributaries. Languages: Shoshoni (Newe — Uto-Aztecan, Numic branch — related to Comanche, Northern Paiute) and Bannock (Northern Paiute — Uto-Aztecan). Shoshoni endangered; Bannock severely endangered. Revitalization active.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Snake River Plain; Portneuf River; Bear River; Boise River; upper Snake River; southern Idaho; northern Nevada; western Wyoming

tribal_nations.name: Shoshone-Paiute Tribes of the Duck Valley Reservation
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Duck Valley Reservation, Owyhee County, Idaho and Elko County, Nevada; straddles ID-NV state line
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Separate sovereign. The Duck Valley Reservation straddles the Idaho-Nevada border — demonstrating the arbitrary nature of state lines imposed across sovereign tribal territory. Two peoples: Western Shoshone (Newe — specifically the Agai-Dicutta 'Salmon Eaters' and Bohogande 'Cattail Eaters' bands) and Northern Paiute (Numa — specifically bands displaced from their territory onto Duck Valley). The reservation was established 1877 by Executive Order. The Western Shoshone never signed a land cession treaty — the U.S. government claimed their lands through the Treaty of Ruby Valley 1863, which the Western Shoshone interpret as a treaty of peace and friendship, not land cession. This legal dispute generated one of the longest-running Indian land claims cases in U.S. history (Western Shoshone National Council v. United States). Mary and Carrie Dann — Western Shoshone sisters — spent decades fighting BIA cattle seizures on their ancestral land in one of the most celebrated Indigenous land rights cases of the late 20th century. Languages: Western Shoshoni (Uto-Aztecan, Numic); Northern Paiute (Numa — Uto-Aztecan). Both endangered.
tribal_nations.treaty_basis: Treaty of Ruby Valley 1863 (15 Stat. 693) — Western Shoshone interpret as peace/friendship only, not land cession; Executive Order reservation 1877
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Owyhee Plateau; Duck Valley; Bruneau River; Jarbidge Mountains; Great Basin high desert straddling ID and NV
tribal_nations.historical_note: Mary and Carrie Dann — Western Shoshone elders — resisted BIA cattle seizures for decades, asserting that their ancestral land was never lawfully ceded. Their case reached international human rights bodies. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights ruled in 2002 that the United States violated Western Shoshone human rights.

tribal_nations.name: Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Primarily Utah-Idaho border area; Brigham City UT headquarters; tribal members across southern Idaho
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Separate sovereign. Primarily based in Utah but included in Idaho context due to traditional territory. The Northwestern Band are the survivors of the Bear River Massacre of January 29, 1863 — when Colonel Patrick Connor and the California Volunteers attacked a Shoshone winter encampment on the Bear River in what is now southern Idaho. At least 250-500 men, women, and children were killed — the largest mass killing of Native people in American history. Colonel Connor received a promotion. The federal government did not formally acknowledge the massacre for 130 years. The site is on the National Register of Historic Places. Language: Shoshoni (Uto-Aztecan, Numic). Endangered. Revitalization active.
tribal_nations.treaty_basis: Treaty of Box Elder 1863 — signed weeks after the Bear River Massacre
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Bear River drainage; Cache Valley; upper Snake River; southern Idaho; northern Utah
tribal_nations.historical_note: Bear River Massacre, January 29, 1863: At least 250 Shoshone people — most estimates far higher — were killed by U.S. Army troops in what is now Franklin County, Idaho. The largest mass killing of Native people in American history. Colonel Connor received a brevet promotion to Brigadier General.
tribal_nations.address: 707 N Main St, Brigham City UT 84302
