tribal_nations.name: Angoon Community Association
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Angoon, Admiralty Island, Southeast Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Tlingit people — Deisheetaan (Beaver clan) and other clans. Angoon is one of the oldest permanently occupied sites in Southeast Alaska. The U.S. Navy bombarded Angoon in 1882 — destroying 40 canoes and most of the village's winter food supply — in retaliation for Tlingit demands for compensation after a company accident killed a shaman. The government paid $90,000 in reparations 97 years later, in 1973. Language: Tlingit (Na-Dene / Athabaskan-Eyak-Tlingit family). Endangered. Revitalization active.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Admiralty Island (Kootznoowoo — 'fortress of bears'); Chatham Strait

tribal_nations.name: Craig Community Association
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Craig, Prince of Wales Island, Southeast Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Haida and Tlingit people of Craig area on Prince of Wales Island. Languages: Haida (language isolate — no known relatives); Tlingit (Na-Dene). Both endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Prince of Wales Island, southeastern Alaska

tribal_nations.name: Douglas Indian Association
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Douglas Island, adjacent to Juneau, Southeast Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Tlingit Auk Kwaan people. Douglas Island is part of the traditional Auk Kwaan territory adjacent to present-day Juneau. Language: Tlingit. Endangered. Revitalization active.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Douglas Island; Gastineau Channel; Lynn Canal region

tribal_nations.name: Hoonah Indian Association
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Hoonah, Chichagof Island, Southeast Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Xunaa (Huna) Tlingit people. Hoonah is the largest Tlingit village in Alaska. The Huna Tlingit were displaced from Glacier Bay by advancing glaciers and returned after glacial retreat — their oral history of this migration is confirmed by geological record. Glacier Bay National Park overlaps with their ancestral territory; access rights were long contested. Language: Tlingit. Endangered. Revitalization active.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Chichagof Island; Glacier Bay (Sit' Eeti Gheeyí — 'the bay in place of the glacier'); Icy Strait

tribal_nations.name: Hydaburg Cooperative Association
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Hydaburg, Prince of Wales Island, Southeast Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Kaigani Haida people — the southernmost branch of the Haida Nation. The Haida are known worldwide for their art, totem poles, and ocean-going canoes. Language: Haida (Kaigani dialect — language isolate, no known relatives). Severely endangered — one of the most endangered languages in North America. Intense revitalization efforts across Alaska and British Columbia Haida communities.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Southern Prince of Wales Island; Dixon Entrance; Dall Island

tribal_nations.name: Central Council of the Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Statewide Alaska; headquarters Juneau; serves Tlingit and Haida people statewide including urban areas
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. The Central Council represents over 32,000 Tlingit and Haida tribal citizens statewide — the largest tribal organization in Southeast Alaska. Founded 1935 to pursue land claims — fought for decades for compensation for the National Forest lands taken from Southeast Alaska tribes without compensation. Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act 1971 provided some compensation but is widely regarded as insufficient and as having permanently altered the structure of Alaska Native land rights. The CCTHITA operates major social service programs, housing, and advocacy statewide. Languages: Tlingit (Na-Dene — endangered, revitalization active); Haida (isolate — severely endangered). Both have active revitalization programs.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Southeast Alaska panhandle from Yakutat south to Dixon Entrance; Alexander Archipelago; adjacent British Columbia
tribal_nations.address: 320 W Willoughby Ave Suite 300, Juneau AK 99801

tribal_nations.name: Organized Village of Kake
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Kake, Kupreanof Island, Southeast Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Ḵéex' Ḵwáan Tlingit people. Kake is one of the larger Southeast Alaska Native communities. Language: Tlingit. Endangered. Revitalization active.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Kupreanof Island; Frederick Sound; Keku Strait

tribal_nations.name: Organized Village of Kasaan
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Kasaan, Prince of Wales Island, Southeast Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Haida people — specifically the Kaigani Haida of Kasaan area. Kasaan is the site of one of the best-preserved totem pole collections in Alaska. Language: Haida. Severely endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Eastern Prince of Wales Island; Kasaan Bay

tribal_nations.name: Klawock Cooperative Association
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Klawock, Prince of Wales Island, Southeast Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Tlingit and Haida people of Klawock. Klawock has a significant collection of totem poles including poles repatriated from the 1909 Alaska-Yukon-Pacific Exposition. Languages: Tlingit, Haida. Both endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Western Prince of Wales Island; Klawock Inlet
tribal_nations.regional_corporation: Klawock Cooperative Association village corp; Sealaska (regional)

tribal_nations.name: Metlakatla Indian Community
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Annette Island, Southeast Alaska — Alaska's only Indian reserve
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Tsimshian people — the only Alaska tribe with a reservation in the traditional sense. In 1887, Anglican missionary William Duncan led approximately 800 Tsimshian people from British Columbia to Annette Island, Alaska, where they established Metlakatla. Congress set aside Annette Island as a reserve in 1891 — the only Indian reserve ever established in Alaska. The Tsimshian are known for their sophisticated art traditions, including button blankets, totem poles, and elaborate ceremony. Language: Sm'algyax (Coast Tsimshian — Tsimshianic family). Endangered. Revitalization active with BC Tsimshian communities.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Annette Island and adjacent waters; traditional Tsimshian territory primarily in British Columbia
tribal_nations.regional_corporation: Annette Island Reserve (unique status — no ANC)

tribal_nations.name: Pelican Tribal Association
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Pelican, Chichagof Island, Southeast Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Tlingit people of Pelican. Language: Tlingit. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Lisianski Inlet; Chichagof Island

tribal_nations.name: Petersburg Indian Association
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Petersburg, Mitkof Island, Southeast Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Tlingit people of Petersburg area. Language: Tlingit. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Mitkof Island; Wrangell Narrows; Frederick Sound
tribal_nations.regional_corporation: Tlingit-Haida Regional Electrical Authority area; Sealaska (regional)

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Saxman
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Saxman, adjacent to Ketchikan, Southeast Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Tlingit people — primarily Cape Fox Corporation area, with some Tsimshian members. Saxman has one of the largest collections of standing totem poles in the world — many repatriated from abandoned villages. Language: Tlingit. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Revillagigedo Island; Tongass Narrows; Cape Fox area

tribal_nations.name: Sitka Tribe of Alaska
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Sitka, Baranof Island, Southeast Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Sheet'ká Kwáan Tlingit people. Sitka — known in Tlingit as Sheet'ká (Shee Atiká — 'the place on the outside of Baranof Island's Shee') — is one of the most historically significant Alaska Native sites. Russian colonizers established the Russian-American Company capital here; the Battle of Sitka (1804) between Tlingit warriors and Russian-Aleut forces was one of the last major armed conflicts between Indigenous people and European colonizers in Alaska. The Tlingit held the fort for six days before withdrawing. Alaska became U.S. territory in 1867. Language: Tlingit. Endangered. Sitka has one of the most active language programs in Southeast Alaska.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Baranof Island; Sitka Sound; West Chichagof Island; Kruzof Island (volcano — Edgecumbe, called L'úx by Tlingit)
tribal_nations.historical_note: Battle of Sitka (Shís'gi Noow) 1804: The Tlingit constructed a fort (Shís'gi Noow — 'sapling fort') and held off Russian-Aleut forces for six days before strategic withdrawal. Marks the last major armed Tlingit resistance to Russian colonization.

tribal_nations.name: Skagway Traditional Council
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Skagway, northern Southeast Alaska; Lynn Canal
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Tlingit people of the upper Lynn Canal — gateway to the Chilkoot Trail. The Chilkoot Trail was a traditional Tlingit trade route long before the 1898 Gold Rush. The Chilkat Tlingit controlled this corridor and traded with interior Athabaskan peoples for generations. Language: Tlingit. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Upper Lynn Canal; Taiya Inlet; Chilkoot and White Pass routes into interior

tribal_nations.name: Wrangell Cooperative Association
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Wrangell, Wrangell Island, Southeast Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Stikine Tlingit people (Ḵaachx̱aana.áak'w Ḵwáan — 'people of the little lake'). Wrangell is one of the oldest communities in Alaska — occupied continuously for at least 10,000 years. Ancient Tlingit petroglyphs on the beach date back thousands of years. The Stikine River was a major trade corridor into the interior. Language: Tlingit. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Wrangell Island; lower Stikine River; Stikine Flats; Zimovia Strait

tribal_nations.name: Yakutat Tlingit Tribe
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Yakutat, Gulf of Alaska coast, northernmost Southeast Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Yaakwdáat Ḵwáan Tlingit people — 'people of Yakutat.' At the northern boundary of Southeast Alaska, Yakutat sits at the edge of the vast Wrangell–St. Elias wilderness. The Yakutat Tlingit historically ranged into the interior, trading with Athabaskan peoples via the Alsek River corridor. Language: Tlingit (Yakutat/Coastal Tlingit dialect). Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Yakutat Bay; Disenchantment Bay; Russell Fjord; Alsek River corridor into St. Elias Mountains

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Chenega
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Chenega Bay, Prince William Sound, Southcentral Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Chugach Alutiiq (Sugpiaq) people. Chenega was devastated by the 1964 Good Friday Earthquake and tsunami — the original village was destroyed, killing 23 of its 68 residents. The community was rebuilt at Chenega Bay. Then in 1989, the Exxon Valdez oil spill contaminated the waters of Prince William Sound — directly impacting Chenega's subsistence way of life. The community has faced two catastrophic environmental disasters within one generation. Language: Alutiiq/Sugpiaq (Yupik branch — Eskimo-Aleut family). Critically endangered. Revitalization active.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Prince William Sound; Chenega Island; Knight Island Passage; western PWS islands
tribal_nations.historical_note: 1964: Good Friday Earthquake tsunami destroyed Chenega village, killing 1/3 of residents. 1989: Exxon Valdez oil spill contaminated the tribe's subsistence territory in Prince William Sound.

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Eyak (Cordova)
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Cordova, Prince William Sound, Southcentral Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. The Eyak people are among the most culturally distinct Alaska Native peoples. The Eyak language is a language isolate within the Na-Dene family — closest relative is the Athabaskan languages, but distinctly its own branch. The Eyak were the ancestral connection between Tlingit/Athabaskan cultures and the Gulf of Alaska. The Eyak language had one last fluent native speaker — Marie Smith Jones (Udach' Kuqax*a'a'ch) — who died in 2008. She spent her final years working tirelessly with linguist Michael Krauss and others to document the language. Eyak is now being revitalized through documentation — it will not die if Eyak people choose to reclaim it. The Exxon Valdez oil spill (1989) devastated Eyak subsistence territory in Prince William Sound.
tribal_nations.language_family: Na-Dene (Eyak — distinct branch, closest to Athabaskan)
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Copper River Delta; Controller Bay; Prince William Sound eastern shore; Kayak Island
tribal_nations.historical_note: Marie Smith Jones, last fluent Eyak speaker, died January 21, 2008. She said: 'My people, they are gone. In another life maybe I will find them.' Eyak language documentation is now complete and revitalization is underway.

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Tatitlek
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Tatitlek, Prince William Sound, Southcentral Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Chugach Alutiiq (Sugpiaq) people. Tatitlek is one of the villages closest to the path of the Exxon Valdez oil spill (1989). The contamination of their subsistence fishing and hunting grounds was devastating to their way of life and cultural practices tied to the land and sea. Language: Alutiiq (Sugpiaq / Chugach dialect). Critically endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Eastern Prince William Sound; Tatitlek Narrows; Bligh Island area
tribal_nations.historical_note: Exxon Valdez oil spill (1989) directly contaminated Tatitlek's subsistence territory.

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Port Graham
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Port Graham, southern Kenai Peninsula, Southcentral Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Alutiiq (Sugpiaq) people of the southern Kenai Peninsula. Language: Alutiiq (Sugpiaq / Pacific Yupik). Critically endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Southern Kenai Peninsula; Kachemak Bay; Cook Inlet outer coast
tribal_nations.regional_corporation: Port Graham Corporation (village); Chugach Alaska Corporation (regional)

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Nanwalek
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Nanwalek (English Bay), southern Kenai Peninsula, Southcentral Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Alutiiq (Sugpiaq) people. Nanwalek is one of the few Alaska Native communities where Alutiiq is still spoken conversationally by community members. Language: Alutiiq (Sugpiaq). Critically endangered but stronger here than in many communities.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Southern Kenai Peninsula; Kachemak Bay outer coast; Resurrection Bay area
tribal_nations.regional_corporation: English Bay Corporation; Chugach Alaska Corporation (regional)

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Akhiok
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Akhiok, Kodiak Island, Southcentral Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Koniag Alutiiq (Sugpiaq) people of Kodiak Island. Akhiok is among the oldest inhabited sites on Kodiak Island — over 7,000 years of continuous occupation. The community was relocated from Old Kaguyak after the 1964 earthquake. Language: Alutiiq (Koniag dialect). Critically endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Southern Kodiak Island; Aliulik Peninsula

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Karluk
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Karluk, western Kodiak Island, Southcentral Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Koniag Alutiiq people. Karluk was once one of the most productive salmon rivers in Alaska — the Karluk River hosted enormous sockeye runs. Commercial overfishing in the late 1800s devastated the runs and the community's subsistence base. Language: Alutiiq. Critically endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Western Kodiak Island; Karluk River drainage; Shelikof Strait coast

tribal_nations.name: Kodiak Area Native Association (KANA)
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Kodiak Island Borough; hub for all Kodiak area villages
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized tribal organization. The Koniag Alutiiq (Sugpiaq) people of the Kodiak Archipelago have lived on these islands for at least 7,000-10,000 years. The Russian colonization of Kodiak (1784) brought catastrophic violence — Alexander Baranov and the Russian-American Company enslaved Alutiiq people, forcing men to hunt sea otters across the North Pacific, separating families, and causing population collapse. The Three Saints Bay massacre (1784) marked the beginning of Russian occupation. By the mid-1800s, the Koniag population had been reduced by 80-90%. The Alutiiq people survived, maintained their identity, and today lead one of the most dynamic cultural revitalization movements in Alaska, including the Alutiiq Museum in Kodiak. Language: Alutiiq (Koniag dialect — Sugpiaq). Critically endangered with active revitalization.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Kodiak Archipelago; Alaska Peninsula coast; Trinity Islands
tribal_nations.historical_note: Russian colonization 1784: The Three Saints Bay massacre initiated Russian colonial occupation. Koniag population reduced by 80-90% through violence, disease, and forced labor across 60 years of Russian-American Company rule.

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Larsen Bay
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Larsen Bay, western Kodiak Island
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Koniag Alutiiq people. Larsen Bay was the site of a significant repatriation case — the Smithsonian Institution had held the skeletal remains of over 1,000 Alutiiq people collected from the Uyak Bay burial sites without consent. After years of advocacy by Larsen Bay residents and KANA, the remains were repatriated in 1991 — one of the first major repatriations under NAGPRA. Language: Alutiiq. Critically endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Uyak Bay; western Kodiak Island
tribal_nations.historical_note: 1991: Larsen Bay Tribal Council successfully negotiated the repatriation of 756 ancestral remains and 2,600 funerary objects from the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History — one of the first major repatriations in U.S. history, predating and helping shape NAGPRA.
tribal_nations.regional_corporation: Larsen Bay Tribal Council village corp; Koniag Inc. (regional)

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Old Harbor
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Old Harbor, southeastern Kodiak Island
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Koniag Alutiiq people. Old Harbor (Nuniaq) is one of the oldest inhabited sites on Kodiak Island. The village was destroyed by the 1964 tsunami but rebuilt. Language: Alutiiq. Critically endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Southeastern Kodiak Island; Sitkalidak Island; Ugak Bay
tribal_nations.regional_corporation: Old Harbor Native Corporation; Koniag Inc. (regional)

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Ouzinkie
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Ouzinkie, Spruce Island, near Kodiak Island
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Koniag Alutiiq people of Spruce Island. Spruce Island (Ouzinkie — from Russian for 'narrow place') is notable as the home of the Russian Orthodox St. Herman, who was canonized as Alaska's first Orthodox saint. Orthodox Christianity became deeply intertwined with Alutiiq identity and culture. Language: Alutiiq. Critically endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Spruce Island; Near Island group; northern Kodiak Island coast

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Port Lions
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Port Lions, Kodiak Island, Southcentral Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Koniag Alutiiq people — relocated from Afognak Island after the 1964 earthquake and tsunami destroyed the original village. The relocation itself was traumatic, separating the community from their ancestral lands on Afognak. Language: Alutiiq. Critically endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Afognak Island (original); northern Kodiak Island area

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Eklutna
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Eklutna, Matanuska-Susitna Borough, near Anchorage, Southcentral Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Dena'ina Athabaskan people — one of the few Athabaskan nations with traditional territory on a saltwater coast (Cook Inlet). The Dena'ina call the area around present-day Anchorage 'Dgheyay Kaq' — 'the place where we got something from the bay.' The Native Village of Eklutna holds the oldest cemetery still in use in the Anchorage area — a sacred site where traditional Dena'ina grave houses blend with Russian Orthodox Christianity. The creek that runs through Eklutna was diverted for Anchorage's water supply — decades of legal battles resulted in a 1991 agreement for fish passage. Language: Dena'ina (Athabaskan family). Severely endangered. Revitalization active.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Dgheyay Kaq' (Anchorage area); Eklutna Lake and River; upper Knik Arm; Matanuska Valley
tribal_nations.regional_corporation: Eklutna Inc.; CIRI — Cook Inlet Region Inc. (regional)

tribal_nations.name: Knik Tribe
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Knik-Wasilla area, Matanuska-Susitna Borough, Southcentral Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Dena'ina Athabaskan people of the Knik Arm area. The Knik area was a major trading center before European contact. Language: Dena'ina. Severely endangered. Revitalization active.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Knik Arm; upper Cook Inlet; Susitna River lower reaches; Matanuska River mouth

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Seldovia
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Seldovia, southern Kenai Peninsula, Kachemak Bay, Southcentral Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Dena'ina Athabaskan and Alutiiq people of the southern Kenai Peninsula. Seldovia was a significant trading post and later cannery town. Language: Dena'ina (severely endangered); Alutiiq (critically endangered). Both with revitalization efforts.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Kachemak Bay south shore; outer Kenai Peninsula; southern Cook Inlet

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Tyonek
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Tyonek, western shore of Cook Inlet, accessible only by air or boat
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Dena'ina Athabaskan people — one of the more traditional and remote Cook Inlet Dena'ina communities. Tyonek is accessible only by small aircraft or boat — no road access. In 1965, oil and gas leases on Tyonek's allotted lands generated $12.9 million, which the tribe used to build modern community infrastructure — at the time one of the wealthiest tribal communities per capita in Alaska. The community has maintained strong ties to subsistence practices. Language: Dena'ina (Upper Inlet dialect). Severely endangered. Strong revitalization program.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Western Cook Inlet shore; Chuitna River drainage; McArthur River area; Beluga area

tribal_nations.name: Copper River Native Association
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Copper River Basin, Southcentral Alaska; Glennallen hub
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized regional tribal organization. Ahtna Athabaskan people (Atna' — 'ice people' or 'Copper River people'). The Ahtna homeland is the Copper River basin — a vast wilderness of glacier-fed rivers, mountains, and taiga. The Copper River itself — called Atna' Bene ('Copper River') — is named for the copper deposits the Ahtna mined and traded for thousands of years. Ahtna copper was a prestige trade good across the Pacific Northwest and Interior. The Wrangell–St. Elias region is among the most intact wilderness ecosystems remaining in North America. Language: Ahtna (Athabaskan family). Severely endangered. Active revitalization.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Copper River basin entire extent; Wrangell Mountains; Talkeetna Mountains; Chitina River; Sanford River; Nabesna River

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Chitina
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Chitina, Copper River area, Southcentral Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Ahtna Athabaskan people — specifically the Tatl'ahwt'aene band ('people of the Chitina River'). Chitina sits at the confluence of the Chitina and Copper Rivers — a location that has been strategically important for salmon fishing for thousands of years. The Kennecott Copper Mine (1903-1938), built on Ahtna territory, extracted $200 million in copper with minimal benefit to the Ahtna people. Language: Ahtna. Severely endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Chitina River drainage; Copper River confluence; Wrangell foothills

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Gakona
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Gakona, Copper River area, Southcentral Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Ahtna Athabaskan people. Gakona is at the confluence of the Gakona and Copper Rivers — a traditional fishing and gathering site. Language: Ahtna. Severely endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Gakona River; Copper River upper reaches; Gulkana River confluence

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Gulkana
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Gulkana, Copper River area, Southcentral Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Ahtna Athabaskan people. Gulkana is near the headwaters of the Copper River system, close to the geographic center of the Ahtna homeland. The Gulkana River has one of the last remaining healthy red salmon runs in the Copper River system. Language: Ahtna. Severely endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Gulkana River drainage; upper Copper River; Alaska Range foothills

tribal_nations.name: Fairbanks Native Association
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Fairbanks, Interior Alaska; urban hub for Interior Athabaskan peoples
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized tribal organization. Tanana Athabaskan people and pan-tribal urban membership. Fairbanks sits in the Tanana River valley — Dena (meaning 'people' in multiple Athabaskan dialects) have lived here for thousands of years. The Fairbanks gold rush of 1902 brought a massive influx of settlers onto Athabaskan territory. FNA provides comprehensive services to urban Native people throughout Interior Alaska. Language: Tanana Athabaskan (multiple dialects — severely to critically endangered). Active revitalization programs at University of Alaska Fairbanks.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Tanana River valley; Chena River; Goldstream Valley; interior subarctic taiga

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Nenana
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Nenana, Tanana River, Interior Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Koyukon and Tanana Athabaskan people. Nenana is known for the Nenana Ice Classic — a tradition since 1917 where people bet on when the Tanana River ice will break up, with winnings historically funding community needs. The ice breakup date is itself a traditional ecological indicator used by Indigenous people for millennia. Language: Koyukon; Tanana. Both severely endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Nenana River confluence with Tanana; Tanana Flats; Alaska Range foothills

tribal_nations.name: Tanana Chiefs Conference
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Interior Alaska — 37 member villages across 235,000 square miles
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized regional tribal organization. TCC represents 37 Interior Alaska Athabaskan villages — Koyukon, Tanana, Tanacross, Upper Tanana, Han, Deg Xinag (Deg Hit'an), Holikachuk, and Gwich'in peoples. The TCC territory encompasses approximately 235,000 square miles — larger than most U.S. states. In 1915, the Tanana Chiefs met at Fairbanks to assert their rights and demand that the government address their situation — one of the earliest formal assertions of Alaska Native sovereignty. That tradition of organized advocacy continues through TCC today. Languages: All Interior Athabaskan languages — Koyukon, Tanana, Tanacross, Upper Tanana, Han, Deg Xinag, Holikachuk, Gwich'in — are endangered or severely endangered. TCC's Heritage Language Program is one of the most comprehensive Native language programs in Alaska.
tribal_nations.language_name: Koyukon; Tanana; Tanacross; Upper Tanana; Han; Deg Xinag; Holikachuk; Gwich'in
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Interior Alaska subarctic: Yukon River middle and upper reaches; Tanana River entire extent; Koyukuk River; Chandalar River; Porcupine River

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Minto
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Minto, Tanana River area, Interior Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Tanana Athabaskan people — Menhti Kenaga ('those who are there at the flats'). Minto is one of the most traditional Interior Alaska communities. The Minto Flats — a vast wetland system — is one of the most productive waterfowl areas in Alaska. The community was relocated in the 1960s from its original location when the Alaska Railroad flooded access routes. Language: Lower Tanana Athabaskan. Severely endangered. One of the most active revitalization efforts in Interior Alaska — the village has produced prominent language teachers and documentation specialists.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Minto Flats; Tolovana River; lower Tanana River; Chatanika River

tribal_nations.name: Gwich'in Steering Committee
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Northeastern Interior Alaska and northern Yukon; Arctic Village, Venetie, Fort Yukon, and other Gwich'in communities
tribal_nations.notes: The Gwich'in (Vadzaih Googii Vi Gwich'in — 'caribou people') are a circumpolar Athabaskan people spanning northeastern Alaska and northwestern Canada. Their entire way of life — physical, spiritual, cultural — is centered on the Porcupine caribou herd. The Porcupine herd calves in the coastal plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR) — which the Gwich'in call 'the sacred place where life begins.' Decades of Gwich'in resistance have made them internationally known as defenders of ANWR. The Gwich'in Steering Committee, established 1988, coordinates advocacy across all Gwich'in communities. Language: Gwich'in (Athabaskan family — related to but distinct from other Athabaskan languages). Endangered. Strong revitalization across Alaska and Yukon/NWT communities.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Northeastern Alaska: Chandalar River; Porcupine River; upper Yukon Flats; Arctic foothills; extending into Yukon and NWT Canada
tribal_nations.historical_note: The Gwich'in have led international resistance to oil development in ANWR since 1988. Their fight is among the longest-running and most visible Indigenous environmental rights campaigns in North America.
tribal_nations.regional_corporation: Doyon Limited (regional); Arctic Village Council; Venetie Tribal Government

tribal_nations.name: Orutsararmiut Native Council (Bethel)
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Bethel, Yukon-Kuskokwim delta, Western Alaska; regional hub
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Central Alaskan Yup'ik people — Orutsararmiut means 'the people from the mountains and mudflats.' Bethel is the largest community in the Yukon-Kuskokwim (YK) delta region and serves as the hub for approximately 56 predominantly Yup'ik villages across 75,000 square miles. The YK delta is one of the largest river deltas in North America and one of the most important waterfowl and salmon habitats on earth. Yup'ik people have lived here for at least 10,000 years, developing extraordinarily sophisticated adaptations to the subarctic coastal environment. Language: Central Alaskan Yup'ik (Yup'ik — Eskimo-Aleut family). Endangered in some communities, still strong in others — one of the healthier Indigenous languages in Alaska with several thousand speakers remaining. Active bilingual education programs.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Kuskokwim River delta; central YK delta; Kuskokwim Bay

tribal_nations.name: Algaaciq Native Village (St. Mary's)
tribal_nations.service_area_description: St. Mary's, Andreafsky River, Yukon-Kuskokwim area, Western Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Central Alaskan Yup'ik people. St. Mary's is a Jesuit mission community — the intersection of Yup'ik traditional culture and Russian Orthodox/Catholic mission history is deeply embedded across the YK delta. Language: Central Alaskan Yup'ik. Endangered to vital.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Andreafsky River; lower Yukon River right bank

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of St. Paul Island
tribal_nations.service_area_description: St. Paul Island, Pribilof Islands, Bering Sea
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Unangan (Aleut) people of the Pribilof Islands. The Unangan of St. Paul Island have one of the most extraordinary histories of any Alaska Native community. The Russian-American Company forcibly transported Unangan people from the Aleutian Islands to the Pribilof Islands in the 1780s to harvest fur seals — effectively creating a labor colony. After the U.S. purchased Alaska in 1867, the federal government continued this system under the Alaska Commercial Company and later the federal government itself — Unangan people were restricted to the islands, required to harvest seals, and controlled by federal agents until 1966. The Unangan of the Pribilofs received a formal congressional apology in 1983 for their treatment during WWII (evacuation to internment camps in southeastern Alaska). Language: Unangan/Aleut (Pribilof dialect — Eskimo-Aleut, Aleut branch). Critically endangered. Revitalization active.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Pribilof Islands (St. Paul and St. George); Bering Sea; traditional Unangan territory primarily Aleutian Islands
tribal_nations.historical_note: 1942: All Unangan people evacuated from Pribilof Islands to substandard camps in southeastern Alaska. Conditions were so poor that many died. The government paid Unangan harvesters 8 cents per fur seal skin. Congressional apology 1983.

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Unalaska
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Unalaska Island (Dutch Harbor), Eastern Aleutian Islands, Southwestern Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Unangan (Aleut) people — Ounalashka, 'near the peninsula.' Dutch Harbor is the busiest fishing port in the United States by tonnage — yet the Unangan people who have lived on this island for over 9,000 years have seen little benefit from this industrial fishery. Russian colonization of the Aleutians beginning in the 1740s was one of the most brutal episodes of colonialism in North American history — the Russian promyshlenniki enslaved Unangan men, took women and children hostage, and caused a population collapse of 80-90% within a generation. Language: Unangan/Aleut (Eastern dialect). Critically endangered — among the most endangered languages in North America. The Aleut language has fewer than 150 remaining speakers across all dialects. Revitalization active at Unalaska and across Aleutian communities.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Unalaska Island; Fox Islands group; eastern Aleutian chain; Bering Sea and Pacific coast
tribal_nations.historical_note: Russian promyshlenniki colonization 1741-1867: Population collapse of 80-90%. The Aleut Evacuation and Internment (1942-1945) during WWII further devastated communities and resulted in Congressional apology and reparations in 1988.

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Atka
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Atka Island, Central Aleutian Islands, Southwestern Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Unangan (Aleut) people — one of the most remote permanently inhabited communities in the United States. Atka speaks the western dialect of Unangan — more distinct from the eastern dialects. WWII evacuation devastated the original community at Nazan Bay; people returned to find their village burned by U.S. forces to deny it to the Japanese. Language: Unangan (Atkan/Western dialect). Critically endangered. Active revitalization — Atka has one of the strongest Unangan language programs in the Aleutians.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Atka Island; Andreanof Islands group; central Aleutian chain
tribal_nations.historical_note: 1942: U.S. forces evacuated all Aleutian communities and burned Atka village themselves to deny it to Japanese forces — returning residents found their homes destroyed not by enemies but by their own government.

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of False Pass
tribal_nations.service_area_description: False Pass (Isanax̂), Unimak Island, Eastern Aleutian Islands
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Unangan (Aleut) people — Isanax̂ ('the place to pass through'). Unimak Island hosts the volcano Shishaldin (Sisquk — 'mountain which points the way when I am lost') — one of the most active volcanoes in Alaska. Language: Unangan. Critically endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Unimak Island; Isanotski Strait; eastern end of Aleutian Chain

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Akutan
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Akutan Island, Fox Islands, Eastern Aleutian Islands
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Unangan (Aleut) people. Akutan Island hosts Akutan Volcano — which produced a significant eruption in 1996 forcing temporary evacuation. The community is adjacent to one of the world's largest seafood processing facilities (Trident Seafoods). Language: Unangan. Critically endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Akutan Island; eastern Fox Islands; Akutan Bay

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Kotzebue
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Kotzebue, Kotzebue Sound, Northwest Arctic Alaska; regional hub
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Inupiaq people — Qikiqtaġruk ('a long peninsula'). Kotzebue is the hub of Northwest Arctic Alaska, serving approximately 11 villages across 35,898 square miles. The Kotzebue region has been inhabited by Inupiaq people for thousands of years — the area was a major trade center where Inupiaq, Athabaskan, Yup'ik, and Siberian peoples exchanged goods. The Maniilaq Association (named for the Inupiaq prophet Maniilaq who predicted the coming of Western people) provides health and social services across the region. Climate change is having catastrophic impacts on Northwest Arctic communities — sea ice loss, coastal erosion, permafrost thaw, and changing subsistence patterns are existential threats. Language: Inupiaq (Northwest Alaska dialect — Eskimo-Aleut, Inuit branch). Endangered. Active revitalization through NANA region schools and Maniilaq.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Kotzebue Sound; Baldwin Peninsula; Kobuk River lower reaches; Hotham Inlet

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Selawik
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Selawik, Selawik Lake area, Northwest Arctic Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Inupiaq people — one of the larger NANA region villages. Selawik National Wildlife Refuge surrounds the community — a vast wetland system critical for caribou, waterfowl, and fish. Language: Inupiaq. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Selawik Lake; Selawik River; Kobuk delta area

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Shungnak
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Shungnak, Kobuk River valley, Northwest Arctic Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Inupiaq people of the Kobuk Valley. The Kobuk Valley has been occupied continuously for over 12,500 years — among the longest records of human occupation in Alaska. Onion Portage archaeological site nearby is one of the most significant in Arctic prehistory. Language: Inupiaq. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Upper Kobuk River valley; Kobuk Valley National Park area; jade deposits

tribal_nations.name: Utqiagvik (Barrow) — North Slope Borough / Inupiat Community of the Arctic Slope
aliases: Inupiat Community of the Arctic Slope
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Utqiaġvik (Barrow), North Slope Borough; northernmost U.S. city; hub for 8 North Slope villages
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Inupiaq people — Utqiaġvik ('the place where snowy owls are hunted'). The North Slope has been inhabited by Inupiaq people for at least 10,000 years. The official name was restored to Utqiaġvik (from Barrow) by municipal vote in 2016 — a landmark act of cultural reclamation. The North Slope sits on the largest oil field in North American history — Prudhoe Bay — discovered 1968. The Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act of 1971 was accelerated by the oil industry's need for clear title to drill. The Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain (adjacent to North Slope) — calving grounds for the Porcupine caribou herd — has been the subject of decades-long drilling debates. Climate change is the most acute threat: sea ice loss, coastal erosion, and permafrost thaw threaten the physical existence of North Slope communities. Elders document how the land and sea are changing beyond anything in living memory. Language: Inupiaq (North Slope dialect — Uqpiagmiutun). Endangered but with several hundred speakers remaining. Strong school-based programs. Alaska Native Language Center (UAF) has extensive Inupiaq documentation.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Arctic Ocean coast from Point Hope to Point Barrow to the Canadian border; Brooks Range north slope; North Slope tundra
tribal_nations.historical_note: 2016: Citizens voted to restore the traditional name Utqiaġvik, replacing the colonial name 'Barrow' — one of the first major Alaska community name restorations.

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Kaktovik
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Kaktovik, Barter Island, Arctic Coast, northeastern Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Inupiaq people of Barter Island — the only community within the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. Kaktovik is at the center of the decades-long ANWR drilling debate. The community is divided on drilling — some members see economic opportunity, others fear impacts on subsistence. Kaktovik is also known for polar bear viewing — a delicate co-existence with bears attracted by bowhead whale bone piles from subsistence hunting. Climate change is visible here in real time — sea ice loss, coastal erosion, and dramatic ecosystem change. Language: Inupiaq. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Barter Island; Arctic Coast; ANWR coastal plain; Canning River to Demarcation Point

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Point Hope
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Point Hope (Tikigaq), Chukchi Sea coast, Northwest Arctic Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Inupiaq people — Tikigaq ('index finger' — describing the long spit of land). Point Hope is one of the oldest continuously inhabited communities in the Western Hemisphere — archaeological evidence suggests at least 2,500 years of continuous occupation, with some estimates reaching back 4,000+ years. The bowhead whale hunt has sustained the community for all of this time. The U.S. government proposed detonating nuclear bombs near Point Hope in 1958-1962 (Project Chariot) to create a harbor — the Inupiaq community organized resistance and the project was cancelled. A radioactive waste site from the project period remained. Language: Inupiaq (North Slope dialect). Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Tikigaq Peninsula; Chukchi Sea coast; Lisburne Peninsula; Cape Thompson
tribal_nations.historical_note: Project Chariot (1958-1962): The Atomic Energy Commission proposed detonating multiple nuclear bombs near Point Hope to create a harbor for coal export. Inupiaq resistance — one of the first successful Indigenous environmental campaigns in American history — stopped the project.

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Gambell
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Gambell, St. Lawrence Island, Bering Sea
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. St. Lawrence Island Yupik (Siberian Yupik) people — Sivuqaq, 'the island squeezed together.' St. Lawrence Island has been inhabited for at least 2,000 years. The St. Lawrence Island Yupik are a circumpolar people — their closest cultural and linguistic relatives are in Siberia, just 40 miles across the Bering Strait. The Cold War divided the Yupik people — families were separated for over 40 years. Visits between Gambell/Savoonga and Siberian Yupik villages resumed in 1988 after the 'Ice Curtain' lifted. St. Lawrence Island Yupik is a distinct language from Central Alaskan Yup'ik — not mutually intelligible. Language: St. Lawrence Island Yupik (Siberian Yupik — Eskimo-Aleut, Yupik branch). Endangered but with an active speaking community. Revitalization active.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: St. Lawrence Island entire extent; Bering Sea; subsistence territory extending into Siberian waters
tribal_nations.historical_note: The Cold War divided the Yupik people — the 'Ice Curtain' separated Alaskan and Siberian Yupik relatives for 40+ years (1948-1988). Family reunification visits resumed when the 'Ice Curtain' lifted.
tribal_nations.regional_corporation: Sivuqaq Inc. (village); Bering Straits Native Corporation (regional)

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Savoonga
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Savoonga, St. Lawrence Island, Bering Sea
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. St. Lawrence Island Yupik people — the second community on St. Lawrence Island. Savoonga is known as the 'walrus capital of the world' — walrus hunting has sustained this community for millennia. Language: St. Lawrence Island Yupik (Siberian Yupik). Endangered but with active speaking community.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: St. Lawrence Island northeastern portion; Bering Sea walrus grounds
tribal_nations.regional_corporation: Savoonga Native Corporation; Bering Straits Native Corporation (regional)

tribal_nations.name: Bristol Bay Native Association
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Bristol Bay region, Southwestern Alaska; approximately 31 member villages
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized regional tribal organization. Bristol Bay is home to Yup'ik, Dena'ina Athabaskan, and Alutiiq peoples. Bristol Bay supports the largest sockeye salmon run on earth — the Nushagak, Kvichak, Naknek, Togiak, and other river systems produce 40-60 million sockeye annually. This fishery has sustained Indigenous peoples here for thousands of years and is the economic foundation of the region. The proposed Pebble Mine project — a massive open-pit gold and copper mine at the headwaters of two of Bristol Bay's most productive salmon rivers — has been vigorously opposed by virtually all tribal governments in the region for decades. Tribal opposition helped defeat Pebble Mine permits. Languages: Central Alaskan Yup'ik (multiple dialects); Dena'ina (Athabaskan); Alutiiq. All endangered to severely endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Bristol Bay drainage: Nushagak, Kvichak, Naknek, Egegik, Ugashik, Togiak rivers; Lake Iliamna; Lake Clark; Wood-Tikchik lakes
tribal_nations.historical_note: Tribal opposition to Pebble Mine: Bristol Bay tribal governments led a decades-long campaign against the Pebble Mine project at the headwaters of the salmon rivers. The EPA used Section 404(c) authority to protect Bristol Bay — one of the most significant tribal environmental victories in Alaska.

tribal_nations.name: Naknek Native Village
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Naknek, Bristol Bay, Southwestern Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Yup'ik and Alutiiq people at the mouth of the Naknek River — gateway to Katmai National Park and one of the world's most productive salmon systems. Language: Central Alaskan Yup'ik; Alutiiq. Both endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Naknek River; Bristol Bay shore; Kvichak Bay

tribal_nations.name: Chilkat Indian Village (Klukwan)
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Klukwan, Chilkat River valley, Southeast Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Chilkat Tlingit people — Jilḵaat Ḵwáan ('people of the Chilkat River'). Klukwan is the cultural heart of the Chilkat Tlingit. The village holds some of the most significant Tlingit art objects in the world — the Whale House interior screen, Raven screen, and other sacred objects were illegally removed in 1984 and are the subject of ongoing repatriation efforts. The Chilkat blanket — one of the most complex textile traditions in North America — originates here. Language: Tlingit. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Chilkat River valley; Lynn Canal; Chilkoot Lake

tribal_nations.name: Ketchikan Indian Community
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Ketchikan, Revillagigedo Island, Southeast Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Tlingit — primarily Tongass Kwaan people with some Haida and Tsimshian members. Ketchikan is the gateway to Southeast Alaska and hosts a significant totem pole collection. Language: Tlingit. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Revillagigedo Island; Tongass Narrows; Ward Cove

tribal_nations.name: Whittier
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Whittier, Passage Canal, Prince William Sound
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Chugach Alutiiq community. Language: Alutiiq. Critically endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Passage Canal; western Prince William Sound

tribal_nations.name: Kenaitze Indian Tribe
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Kenai, Kenai Peninsula, Southcentral Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Dena'ina Athabaskan people — Kenaits'a ('the people of Kenai'). The Kenai Peninsula was Dena'ina territory — one of the only Athabaskan peoples with a coastal adaptation. The Cook Inlet fishery, Kenai River (world-famous for king salmon), and the forests and mountains of the Peninsula have sustained Dena'ina people for thousands of years. The Kenai oil and gas fields — discovered 1957 — dramatically altered the landscape and economy. Language: Dena'ina (Outer Inlet dialect). Severely endangered. Active revitalization.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Kenai Peninsula; Cook Inlet coast; Kenai River; Skilak Lake; Kachemak Bay

tribal_nations.name: Ninilchik Traditional Council
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Ninilchik, Kenai Peninsula, Cook Inlet coast
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Dena'ina Athabaskan people with significant Russian Creole heritage — descendants of Russian-American Company workers who intermarried with Dena'ina. Ninilchik developed a distinctive dialect blending Dena'ina and Russian — Ninilchik Russian, now nearly extinct. Language: Dena'ina (severely endangered); Ninilchik Russian (moribund).
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Lower Kenai Peninsula Cook Inlet coast; Deep Creek; Anchor Point

tribal_nations.name: Anvik Village
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Anvik, lower Yukon River, Interior/Western Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Deg Xinag (Deg Hit'an — 'people of the river bottom') Athabaskan people. One of the southernmost Interior Athabaskan communities, near the transition zone between Athabaskan and Yup'ik territories. Language: Deg Xinag (Athabaskan). Severely endangered — fewer than 20 speakers.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Anvik River; lower Yukon River right bank; Alaska Range foothills

tribal_nations.name: Holy Cross Village
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Holy Cross, lower Yukon River, Interior/Western Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Deg Xinag Athabaskan people with Yup'ik presence. Jesuit mission community — the intersection of Athabaskan culture and Catholic mission tradition. Language: Deg Xinag. Severely endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Lower Yukon River; Innoko River area

tribal_nations.name: Ruby Tribal Council
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Ruby, middle Yukon River, Interior Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Koyukon Athabaskan people. Language: Koyukon (Athabaskan). Severely endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Middle Yukon River; Melozitna River drainage

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Koyukuk
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Koyukuk, Koyukuk River mouth, Interior Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Koyukon Athabaskan people — at the confluence of the Koyukuk and Yukon Rivers. The Koyukuk River drains a vast wilderness of boreal forest and mountains. Language: Koyukon (Athabaskan). Severely endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Koyukuk River mouth; middle Yukon River

tribal_nations.name: Huslia Village
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Huslia, Koyukuk River, Interior Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Koyukon Athabaskan people — one of the most traditional Koyukon communities. The late Chief Henry (Jimmy Huntington) and others documented Koyukon traditional knowledge extensively. Language: Koyukon. Severely endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Koyukuk River middle reaches; Huslia River

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Tanacross
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Tanacross, Tanana River, Interior Alaska near Alaska-Canada border
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Tanacross Athabaskan people — the Tanacross language is a distinct Athabaskan language from Tanana or Upper Tanana. The community sits at a traditional crossroads between Interior and eastern Alaska peoples. Language: Tanacross (Athabaskan). Critically endangered — very few speakers remaining. Active documentation.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Upper Tanana River; Tok area; Mentasta area; White River vicinity

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Tetlin
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Tetlin, upper Tanana River area, Interior Alaska near Alaska-Yukon border
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Upper Tanana Athabaskan people. Tetlin is near the Alaska-Yukon border — the Upper Tanana language connects communities across the international boundary. Traditional travel routes between Tetlin and Yukon First Nations continue to this day. Language: Upper Tanana (Athabaskan). Critically endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Upper Tanana River; Chisana River; Nabesna River area; Alaska-Yukon borderlands

tribal_nations.name: Tok Community Association
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Tok, Tanana River area, Interior Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Upper Tanana Athabaskan people. Language: Upper Tanana. Critically endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Upper Tanana River valley; Tok River

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Eagle
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Eagle, upper Yukon River, Interior Alaska near Alaska-Yukon border
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Han Athabaskan people (Haan Hwech'in — 'people who dwell along the river'). The Han are a Yukon River people whose territory spans the Alaska-Yukon border. The Klondike Gold Rush of 1898 devastated Han communities — Dawson City was built in the heart of Han territory, overwhelming the Indigenous population within months. Language: Han (Athabaskan). Critically endangered — very few speakers. Joint revitalization with Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in First Nation (Dawson City, Yukon).
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Upper Yukon River: from Fortymile River to Dawson area; White River; Forty Mile country
tribal_nations.historical_note: Klondike Gold Rush 1897-1899: The Han homeland became the center of the most intensive gold rush in North American history. Dawson City — built on Han fishing camps — went from zero to 30,000 people in two years.

tribal_nations.name: Nome Eskimo Community
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Nome, Norton Sound, Western Alaska; regional hub
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Inupiaq people — Sitnasuak ('where the water drips'). Nome was established during the 1899-1909 gold rush — the beach was literally covered in gold-seekers who overwhelmed the Inupiaq population. Nome is now the hub for the Norton Sound region, serving approximately 15 surrounding villages. Nome is also the finish line for the Iditarod Sled Dog Race — sled dogs were a central transportation technology of Inupiaq culture. Language: Inupiaq (Norton Sound/Seward Peninsula dialect). Endangered. Revitalization active.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Seward Peninsula coast; Norton Sound; Nome River drainage

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Unalakleet
aliases: Inupiaq and Yup'ik — Norton Sound junction
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Unalakleet, Norton Sound, Western Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Unalakleet is at the historic boundary between Inupiaq and Yup'ik territories — the community has members of both traditions. It was a major trade center. Language: Inupiaq and Central Alaskan Yup'ik. Both endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Unalakleet River; Norton Sound coast; traditional Inupiaq-Yup'ik boundary area

tribal_nations.name: Stebbins Community Association
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Stebbins, Norton Sound, Western Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Yup'ik people. Language: Central Alaskan Yup'ik. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Norton Sound south shore; Shaktoolik River area

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Hooper Bay
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Hooper Bay, Yukon-Kuskokwim delta coast, Western Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Central Alaskan Yup'ik people — Naparyaarmiut ('people of the driftwood pole place'). One of the larger YK delta coastal communities. Subsistence is central — beluga whale, seal, walrus, fish, and waterfowl. Language: Central Alaskan Yup'ik. Vital in this community — one of the stronger Yup'ik-speaking villages.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: YK delta coast; Hazen Bay; Kokechik Bay

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Chevak
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Chevak, YK delta, Western Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Cup'ik people — speakers of Cup'ik, a distinct dialect of Central Alaskan Yup'ik associated with Nunivak Island that also has mainland speakers at Chevak. Cup'ik is distinct enough from Central Yup'ik to sometimes be considered a separate language. Language: Cup'ik. Endangered but with active speakers.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: YK delta; coastal plain near Nelson Island

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Mekoryuk (Nunivak Island)
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Mekoryuk, Nunivak Island, Bering Sea, Western Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Cup'ig people — speakers of Cup'ig, the Nunivak Island dialect of Yup'ik (distinct from Cup'ik and Central Yup'ik). Nunivak Island is the home of the Yup'ik mask-making tradition — masks from Nunivak are among the most significant Indigenous art forms in Alaska. The island was also the site of a 1930s musk ox reintroduction program — musk ox now provide qiviut (wool) for a community knitting cooperative. Language: Cup'ig (Nunivak Cup'ig). Endangered. Revitalization active.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Nunivak Island entire extent; adjacent Bering Sea

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Quinhagak
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Quinhagak, Kuskokwim Bay, Western Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Central Alaskan Yup'ik people. Quinhagak has become internationally known for the Nunalleq archaeological site — an excavation of a Yup'ik village destroyed in a 16th-century raid, which has produced thousands of extraordinary artifacts including wooden objects, masks, and woven grass items rarely preserved elsewhere. Community members participate in the dig and repatriation efforts. Language: Central Alaskan Yup'ik. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Kuskokwim Bay; Kanektok River; Arolik River
tribal_nations.historical_note: Nunalleq archaeological site near Quinhagak: A 16th-century Yup'ik village destroyed in raids, producing extraordinary artifacts in excellent preservation. Community-driven excavation and repatriation model is seen as a gold standard for collaborative archaeology.

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Toksook Bay
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Toksook Bay, Nelson Island, Western Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Central Alaskan Yup'ik people. Nelson Island is a major center of Yup'ik cultural strength — dance, ceremony, and language remain vital here. Toksook Bay was the first location to report 2020 Census results in the United States. Language: Central Alaskan Yup'ik. Vital to endangered — one of the stronger Yup'ik communities.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Nelson Island; Toksook Bay

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Kiana
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Kiana, Kobuk River, Northwest Arctic Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Inupiaq people of the Kobuk River valley. Language: Inupiaq (Kobuk dialect). Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Kobuk River middle reaches; Walker Lake area

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Kobuk
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Kobuk, upper Kobuk River, Northwest Arctic Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Inupiaq people of the upper Kobuk valley — near Kobuk Valley National Park and Great Kobuk Sand Dunes (a remarkable arctic landscape). Language: Inupiaq. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Upper Kobuk River; Kobuk Valley National Park; Great Kobuk Sand Dunes

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Noorvik
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Noorvik, lower Kobuk River delta, Northwest Arctic Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Inupiaq people — one of the larger NANA region villages. Language: Inupiaq. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Kobuk River delta; Selawik Lake area

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Ambler
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Ambler, upper Kobuk River, Northwest Arctic Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Inupiaq people. Ambler is near significant mineral deposits — the proposed Ambler Mining District road has been strongly opposed by tribal governments in the region due to impacts on subsistence and the watershed. Language: Inupiaq. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Upper Kobuk River; Brooks Range foothills south slope

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Anaktuvuk Pass
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Anaktuvuk Pass, Brooks Range, North Slope Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Nunamiut Inupiaq people — 'inland people,' the only Inupiaq group traditionally living in the interior mountains rather than the coast. The Nunamiut were nomadic caribou hunters who followed the caribou herds through the Brooks Range. They were thought by many outsiders to have 'disappeared' by 1900 — in fact they had adapted and continued. Settled at Anaktuvuk Pass in the 1950s, within Gates of the Arctic National Park. The isolation and continuing traditional lifestyle make Nunamiut one of the most culturally distinctive Alaska Native communities. Language: Inupiaq (Nunamiut dialect). Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Brooks Range: Anaktuvuk River drainage; John River; Chandler River; full range of caribou migration routes

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Wainwright
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Wainwright, Chukchi Sea coast, North Slope Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Inupiaq people of the Chukchi Sea coast. Wainwright is a traditional whaling community — the bowhead whale hunt is central to Inupiaq cultural and physical survival. Language: Inupiaq. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Chukchi Sea coast; Kuk River; Wainwright Inlet

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Nuiqsut
aliases: North Slope Inupiaq — Colville River delta
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Nuiqsut, Colville River delta, North Slope Alaska — surrounded by oil fields
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Inupiaq people. Nuiqsut is the community most directly surrounded by North Slope oil development — the village sits within the active Prudhoe Bay and Alpine oil fields. Residents have documented air quality impacts, subsistence disruption, and health concerns from decades of adjacent industrial activity. Despite decades of advocacy, the community continues to face new oil field development on their doorstep. Language: Inupiaq. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Colville River delta; Arctic Ocean coast; Beaufort Sea; inland North Slope
tribal_nations.historical_note: Nuiqsut is the most directly impacted Alaska Native community from North Slope oil development — surrounded by active oil fields with documented air quality, subsistence, and health impacts.

tribal_nations.name: Village of Atqasuk
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Atqasuk, North Slope inland, Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Inupiaq people. One of the smaller North Slope villages. Language: Inupiaq. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Meade River drainage; North Slope tundra

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Point Lay
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Point Lay, Chukchi Sea coast, North Slope Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Inupiaq people. Point Lay is near the Teshekpuk Lake Special Area — critical habitat for caribou and migratory birds. Walrus also haul out near Point Lay in massive numbers due to sea ice loss — a dramatic climate change indicator documented by the community. Language: Inupiaq. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Chukchi Sea coast; Kasegaluk Lagoon; Teshekpuk Lake area

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Aleknagik
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Aleknagik, Wood River Lakes, Bristol Bay area
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Yup'ik people of the Wood River Lakes area — gateway to the Wood-Tikchik State Park, largest state park in the U.S. The Wood River-Tikchik Lakes system is one of the most productive sockeye salmon habitats in the world. Language: Central Alaskan Yup'ik. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Wood River Lakes; Tikchik Lakes; Nushagak River drainage

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Manokotak
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Manokotak, Nushagak River area, Bristol Bay
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Yup'ik people of the lower Nushagak River drainage. Language: Central Alaskan Yup'ik. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Lower Nushagak River; Igushik River; Nushagak Bay

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Togiak
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Togiak, Togiak Bay, Bristol Bay area
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Yup'ik people. Togiak sits at the entrance to Togiak National Wildlife Refuge — one of the most productive coastal wetland systems in Alaska, supporting walrus, salmon, seabirds, and brown bear. Language: Central Alaskan Yup'ik. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Togiak Bay; Togiak River drainage; Cape Newenham; Goodnews Bay area

tribal_nations.name: Egegik Village
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Egegik, Alaska Peninsula, Bristol Bay area
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Alutiiq/Yup'ik people of the Alaska Peninsula. Egegik River is one of the most productive sockeye salmon systems in the Bristol Bay drainage. Language: Alutiiq/Yup'ik. Endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Egegik River drainage; Bristol Bay coast; Alaska Peninsula

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of Pilot Point
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Pilot Point, Alaska Peninsula, Bristol Bay area
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Alutiiq people of the Alaska Peninsula. Language: Alutiiq. Critically endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Alaska Peninsula; Ugashik River; Ugashik Lakes

tribal_nations.name: King Cove Community Association
tribal_nations.service_area_description: King Cove, Alaska Peninsula, near Cold Bay
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Alutiiq people. King Cove has fought for decades to have a road connecting to Cold Bay (which has a major airport) — the lack of road access has cost lives in medical emergencies. The road controversy involves Izembek National Wildlife Refuge and has reached the U.S. Supreme Court. Language: Alutiiq. Critically endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Alaska Peninsula tip; Amak Island; Belkofski Bay

tribal_nations.name: Qagan Tayagungin Tribe of Sand Point Village
tribal_nations.service_area_description: Sand Point, Popof Island, Shumagin Islands, Southwesterm Alaska
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Unangan (Aleut) people — Qagan Tayagungin ('the people of the sun going over a hill'). The Shumagin Islands were named by Vitus Bering after one of his sailors who died and was buried there — the first European buried in Alaska. Language: Unangan. Critically endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: Popof Island; Shumagin Islands; Alaska Peninsula adjacent coast

tribal_nations.name: Native Village of St. George
tribal_nations.service_area_description: St. George Island, Pribilof Islands, Bering Sea
tribal_nations.notes: Federally recognized. Unangan (Aleut) people of St. George Island — the smaller of the two Pribilof Islands. Like St. Paul Island, the St. George community was subjected to the fur seal labor colony system under both Russian and American rule. St. George has the largest seabird colony in the Northern Hemisphere — the cliffs host millions of murres, kittiwakes, puffins, and other birds. Language: Unangan (Pribilof Eastern dialect). Critically endangered.
tribal_nations.traditional_territory: St. George Island; Bering Sea; traditional Unangan territory Aleutian Islands
